hook: The absent-minded Scot who explained how markets work.

pages.x: Adam Smith was born in 1723 in Kirkcaldy, Scotland. A family story says that at three he was carried off by travelling people and rescued. He studied at Glasgow and Oxford, where the teaching was so poor that he taught himself.

He became a professor at Glasgow, famous for being absent-minded. He once walked into a tanning pit while explaining an idea to a friend, and once wandered 24 km in his dressing gown, lost in thought, before church bells brought him back.
In a pin factory, he noted, one worker alone might make 20 pins a day. Ten workers, each doing one step, could make 48,000.
pages.fx: Specialising explains why modern economies are so productive, from factories to world trade.

pages.x: In 1776 he published The Wealth of Nations. When people trade freely, each seeking their own gain, an "invisible hand" leads them to benefit everyone: "It is not from the benevolence of the butcher that we expect our dinner, but from his regard to his own interest."

His first book, The Theory of Moral Sentiments, said people are moved by sympathy for others, and he thought it his better book. He attacked greedy merchants and monopolies, and wanted schools for the poor.
In an irony he enjoyed, the champion of free trade spent his last years as a customs officer in Edinburgh, collecting taxes on imports. He had most of his papers burned before he died in 1790.
Adam Smith is called the father of economics. His ideas on free markets, trade and the division of labour shaped modern economies, and his face was on the Bank of England's 20-pound note.
pts: Explained the "invisible hand" of the market
